answers.flag: Option D (copy open orders to a second table with a stream-triggered Lambda) also removes the scan reads from the main table, so only the unmeasured claim that a sparse GSI has less operational overhead separates E from D.

case.label: D
case.text: D removes the nightly Scan load from the checkout table completely and leaves the checkout API write path and the table's indexes untouched, while E needs the checkout code to set and remove the marker attribute, a backfill of existing open orders, and a key design that the Query can address with an equality condition. D needs a stream, a Lambda function and delete handling, but each piece is managed and small, so a careful candidate can call D equal or lower in risk. The constraint 'least operational overhead' is the only tie-breaker and is not quantified. Wording cues also help the key: 'few orders are open at any time' points at a sparse index, and 'can show data that is a few seconds old' points at eventually consistent reads.

case.label: C
case.text: A TransactWriteItems call with one conditional Put also detects the lost update and rolls back on a failed condition, so it solves the conflict. It is wrong only because a transactional write consumes twice the write capacity of a standard write, and the stem's cost constraint ('as little write capacity as possible') is what excludes it. If a candidate does not know the transaction cost factor, C and A look the same, so the question tests that one fact. The phrase 'MOST cost-effective' with 'as little write capacity as possible' also points straight at the cheaper standard conditional write.
